name: Strava
summary: Strava records sports activities and places them inside a social layer of feeds, followers, clubs, challenges, and segment rankings. The app asks a person to record an activity, then connects that activity to other people through following, kudos, comparison, and shared challenges. Its rankings are scoped to individual segments and to rolling 90-day windows rather than to the whole user base, and its streak is counted in weeks rather than days. A large share of the deeper tracking and mapping features belongs to the paid subscription.

writeup.observed: Strava counts its streak in weeks rather than days, so the state depends on logging an activity inside a 7-day window rather than on returning every day. The streak sits on the home dashboard as your streak, a flame icon with the count enclosed in it, reading zero weeks on a new account. The copy beside it states how to begin, by logging an activity. A view calendar button opens a fuller screen showing the streak activities and the current streak for the month, together with performance across the previous 12 weeks. The qualifying event is recording an activity, the same action the rest of the app is built around.
writeup.presented: The streak is the first item in a 4-item carousel at the top of the home dashboard, directly under the upgrade button. A record button sits beside the view calendar button, so the action that advances the streak is one tap from the place the streak is shown.
writeup.noting: The weekly period is the choice worth noticing. Strava counts weeks on a streak, so a person keeps the state through activity within a week instead of a daily return. The calendar view sets the current count against 12 weeks of prior performance, so the number arrives with history behind it rather than alone. Placing the record button next to the streak display puts the qualifying action in the same place as the state it advances.
findings: Strava measures the streak in weeks, so the state is kept by logging one activity inside a 7-day window.
The qualifying event is recording an activity, which is the same action the rest of the app is built around.
The streak card carries a record button beside the calendar button, putting the action next to the display of the state.
The calendar view shows the current streak against performance from the previous 12 weeks.

screenshots.caption: You tab streak calendar view showing the 12-week history grid, the current month calendar, and the "unlock your full potential" subscription prompt below

writeup.observed: Strava runs many challenges at once and varies the shape of the goal rather than only its size. Within a single month we saw challenges asking for 400 minutes of running, a first 5 km run, 10 active days in a row, and 180 minutes of sweat, alongside others built around swimming, elevation, steps, and a half marathon. Joining takes one tap. Each challenge has its own page carrying the days left, the club organising it, what the challenge asks for, what is earned, and a leaderboard of the people taking part. Completion rewards are frequently digital trophies. Several challenges are organised with named partners, including Runna, Hoka, and Brooks, and the 400 minute running challenge unlocks a 2-week Runna trial on completion. Creating a group challenge or designing a custom challenge is available to subscribers.
writeup.presented: Challenges appear in two places, as a scrollable set of suggested challenges on the dashboard and as a dedicated tab in the Groups area, where they can be filtered by activity type, elevation gain, moving time, and distance. Featured challenges display how many athletes have joined, and the larger ones we saw carried more than 1 million participants each.
writeup.noting: The variety is the design choice worth noticing. The challenges running in one month span total time, a single first distance, consecutive active days, elevation, steps, and swimming, so the set covers several sports and several shapes of goal rather than one. Each challenge states a success condition and a fixed boundary, the first to the last day of the month, so completion is unambiguous. The partner challenges attach a reward that exists outside Strava, a trial of a partner product, alongside the digital trophies the other challenges award.
findings: Strava varies the shape of the goal across a month of challenges, covering total time, a first distance, consecutive active days, elevation, steps, and swimming.
Every challenge states both a success condition and a fixed boundary, so a participant can tell whether they finished.
Joining takes one tap, and each challenge page carries the days remaining, the organising club, and a leaderboard of participants.
Completion rewards are usually digital trophies, while the partner challenges add a trial of a partner product.

writeup.observed: Strava builds its feed out of recorded activities rather than written posts, so items appear without anyone composing them. Each item carries the athlete, the activity data, and any media attached to it. One item we saw showed a ride of almost 34 km with its route, elevation gain, time, and photos, and another carried a video. Every item can take kudos, a one tap reaction, or a comment, and shows how many of each it has already collected along with how many achievements the athlete holds. The top of the feed is given to recommended athletes the viewer does not yet follow. Activities can also be kept out of it, since the visibility controls include not publishing to the home or club feed.
writeup.presented: The feed occupies the lower portion of the home dashboard as one vertically scrolling stream, mixing recommended athletes with activities from people the viewer follows and from other users. Each item shows the athlete, the activity data, any photos or video, and the counts of kudos and comments it has received.
writeup.noting: Generating items from recorded activity removes the step where a person decides what to post. The activity is the content, and it is complete before sharing is considered, with route, distance, elevation, time, and media already attached. Kudos is a one tap reaction, a lighter form of response than writing a comment, and both counts sit on every item. Placing recommended athletes above the followed activity means an account that follows nobody still opens to a populated stream.
findings: Strava builds feed items automatically from recorded activities, so the feed fills without anyone composing a post.
Each item arrives complete with route, distance, elevation, time, and any photos or video from the activity.
Kudos is a one tap reaction and a lighter form of response than a comment, with both counts visible on every item.
Recommended athletes sit at the top of the feed, so an account that follows nobody still opens to a populated stream.

writeup.observed: Strava scopes its rankings to a single stretch of road or trail rather than to the whole app, so a person is compared with the people who covered the same ground. Segments carry ordered lists of the athletes who have run or ridden them, and the app also states where a user stands personally. A Local Legend title marks holding the most efforts on a segment over the previous 90 days, a top 10 view collects the segments where the user places in the first 10, and CRs are the segments where the user holds the best overall time. Challenges carry their own leaderboards, ordering participants by the measure the challenge is built on, such as pace, distance, or steps. Strava also offers a notification for losing a top place, listed in settings as lost CR and lost ratings. Segment leaderboards and best efforts are available to subscribers, so we did not reach the full extent of ranking on a free account.
writeup.presented: Rankings appear as ordered lists inside segment views and on each challenge page, with the measure the ranking uses shown beside each participant. A user's own position is presented separately as a named standing rather than only as a row in a list, with Local Legend, a top 10 collection, and CR holder attached to segments and to a 90-day window.
writeup.noting: Two different things run side by side here, and Strava keeps them apart. The ordered list shows the field, and the named standing states where a person sits in it. Local Legend is the more unusual of the two, because it ranks by how many times someone covered a segment over a rolling 90-day window rather than by how fast they covered it, which makes the top place on a segment a matter of repetition rather than speed. The lost place notification shows the standing is built to be losable, since another athlete's result can take it.
findings: Strava scopes its rankings to individual segments, so the comparison set is the people who covered the same ground.
Local Legend ranks by number of efforts over a rolling 90-day window, which makes the top place a matter of repetition rather than speed.
The app presents a user's own standing as a named title, separately from the ordered list it comes from.
Segment leaderboards and best efforts belong to the subscription, so the free tier shows only part of the ranking system.

writeup.observed: Strava places its first recognitions close to the start. The trophy case opens with the 1st activity, then the 3rd, the 5th, and the 10th, and the same ladder continues up to 1,000. The first trophy arrives immediately after the first activity is saved, as a pop up welcoming the user and marking the activity, offering a choice between viewing the activity and viewing the new trophy in the case. Alongside these count based trophies, Strava marks personal records against a user's own history, and after the first saved ride the app showed a personal record badge reading new best effort, longest ride ever. Completing a named challenge adds a digital trophy to the same case. Other athletes' profiles display how many trophies they hold and at what grade, with counts such as 53 trophies and 10 silver among the ones we saw.
writeup.presented: The trophy case sits at the bottom of the profile, with a view all listing that runs the thresholds up to 1,000 activities. A personal record attaches to the activity that earned it rather than living only in the case. The first activity is marked with a celebratory animation and the welcome pop up, which offers the trophy case as one of its two next steps.
writeup.noting: The spacing of the early thresholds is the notable part. 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 10th activity sit close together at the beginning of a ladder that runs to 1,000. Strava also runs two kinds of recognition next to each other. The trophy case counts activities, a measure that only accumulates. The personal record compares a result against the user's own previous results, so that recognition does not depend on how the user compares with other athletes. The first trophy is given for the first activity, which puts the first recognition at the same moment as the first use of the core action.
findings: Strava's trophy case starts at the 1st activity and marks the 3rd, 5th, and 10th before continuing to 1,000.
The first trophy is awarded for the first saved activity, so recognition begins at the same moment as the core action.
Personal records are measured against a user's own previous results, so this recognition does not depend on comparison with others.
Challenge completions add their digital trophies to the same case, putting two sources of recognition in one place.

writeup.observed: Strava lets any user create a club and gives the creator the controls that decide who gets in. The creation flow runs through 5 steps, choosing the club's sport, picking up to 3 tags describing what the club is for, such as local community, team, or coach led, setting the name, photo, and description, choosing whether the club is public or private, and setting a location. A private club requires people to request permission, and only admins approve new members. Clubs are found through a searchable directory filtered by location and sport, which returned dozens of clubs in the area we searched, and their sizes range widely, with the main Strava club listing almost 7 million athletes. A club page shows its sport, member count, type, events, activities, stats, and posts, and members can create club events with attendance controls. Creating a group challenge inside a club is available to subscribers.
writeup.presented: Clubs appear as a tab in search and as their own area under Groups, presented as a browsable directory. Each club carries a member count and its public or private state, so the size and the entry rules are visible before joining. The creation flow gives the public or private decision its own step, with the consequence stated on that screen.
writeup.noting: The governance controls are the part worth noticing. Strava does not only let a person join a club, it lets them run one, and the private setting with admin approval gives a club a real boundary rather than a label. The tags cover a wide range of purposes, from local community groups to teams, brands, and coach led groups, so one structure serves several different kinds of gathering.
findings: Any user can create a club, and the creation flow includes the decision of whether membership is open or requires admin approval.
Club discovery is filtered by location and sport, so the directory can surface groups in a user's own area.
Club pages carry events, posts, activities, and a member count, giving a club its own surface separate from the main feed.
Creating a group challenge inside a club belongs to the subscription.

system.tagline: Recording an activity is the hub the rest of the system runs on.
system.overview: Strava's system is organised around one action. Recording an activity produces a feed item, can produce a trophy or a personal record, counts toward any challenge the person has joined, advances the weekly streak, and can place the person on a segment ranking. The social layer around that action is built from following relationships, clubs, kudos, and comments.
system.loop: A person records an activity and saves it with a name, a visibility setting, photos, gear, and an effort rating. Saving it publishes an item to the home feed, where other athletes can give kudos or leave a comment. The same saved activity advances the weekly streak, counts toward any challenge the person has joined, and can produce a trophy for reaching an activity count or a personal record for a best effort. If the activity covered a segment, it can also place the person on that segment's ranking. Clubs sit alongside this loop, organising challenges and carrying their own feed. The principle the system is built around is that one recorded activity feeds every other mechanic, so the app only has to ask for the single action it exists to track.
system.keyInsight: The whole system is fed by one action. Strava does not ask a person to post, to check in, or to complete a separate daily task. It asks them to record an activity, and that one event advances the streak, fills the feed, counts toward challenges, can produce a trophy or a personal record, and can place the person on a segment ranking. The mechanics are layered onto the action the product already exists to perform rather than added beside it.
system.whatMakesItWork: Strava keeps its comparisons close to the user. Segment rankings compare people who covered the same stretch of ground, Local Legend counts efforts over a rolling 90-day window rather than all time speed, and personal records compare a result against a user's own history rather than against anyone else. The streak is counted in weeks rather than days, and the first trophies arrive at the 1st, 3rd, and 5th activity. Each of these choices narrows the comparison or shortens the interval rather than widening it.

roles.role: A stream built automatically from recorded activities, carrying kudos, comments, and media, with recommended athletes at the top.
Ordered lists inside segments and challenge pages, plus a user's own standing as Local Legend, top 10, or CR holder.
Month bounded goals with stated success conditions, joined in one tap and rewarded with digital trophies or partner trials.
Trophies for activity count thresholds from the first activity upward, and personal records measured against a user's own history.
User created clubs with member rosters, public or private entry, events, posts, and their own feed.
A count of weeks in which the person logged an activity, advanced by the same action the app is built around.

connections.effect: A single recorded activity moves more than one part of the system at once.
